tracks.name: Game Development
tracks.desc: Learn how games really work by coding their logic in JavaScript — the game loop, movement and gravity, collision detection, score and lives, keyboard controls and simple enemy AI. Then see finished games running the same ideas in the Arcade.
outcomes: Understand and build a game loop
Move objects with position and velocity
Track score, lives and game state

lessons.title: How games actually work: the game loop
lessons.content:
Every game is a loop that never stops (until you quit)

A game does the same three things ~60 times a second: read input, update the world a tiny bit, and draw it. That is called the game loop. Movement looks smooth because each frame changes things only slightly.

function loop() {
  handleInput();
  update();      // move everything a little
  draw();        // paint the new picture
  requestAnimationFrame(loop);  // do it again next frame
}

In this track you'll build the logic of a game and check it with numbers. In the Arcade you can see finished games running this exact loop.

exercises.q: A game runs at 60 frames per second. Print how many frames happen in 3 seconds.
exercises.solution:
let fps=60, seconds=3;
console.log(fps*seconds);

exercises.q: Simulate 5 frames of a loop. Each frame, print 'frame N' (N from 1 to 5).
exercises.solution: for(let f=1;f<=5;f++){ console.log('frame '+f); }

exercises.q: A timer counts down 1 each frame from 3. Print each value until it reaches 0 (3,2,1,0).
exercises.starter:
let t = 3;
// print t each frame until 0
exercises.solution:
let t=3;
while(t>=0){ console.log(t); t--; }

lessons.title: Moving things: position and velocity
lessons.content:
Position + velocity = movement

Every moving object has a position (x, y) and a velocity (how much x and y change each frame). Each frame you just add velocity to position.

let x = 0;
let vx = 5;          // moves 5 pixels right per frame

// each frame:
x = x + vx;          // after 1 frame x=5, after 2 x=10 ...

Gravity is just downward velocity that grows

let y = 0, vy = 0;
// each frame:
vy = vy + 1;   // gravity pulls harder each frame
y = y + vy;    // 1, then 3, then 6, then 10 ... it accelerates

lessons.title: Collision detection
lessons.content:
Do two boxes overlap?

Most game collisions use rectangles (a "hitbox"). Two rectangles overlap when they overlap on both the x axis and the y axis. This is called AABB (axis-aligned bounding box) collision.

function overlap(ax, ay, aw, ah, bx, by, bw, bh) {
  return ax < bx + bw &&
         ax + aw > bx &&
         ay < by + bh &&
         ay + ah > by;
}

Distance for circles

Two circles touch when the distance between their centres is less than the sum of their radii.

exercises.q: Write overlap() and test two boxes that DO overlap: A(0,0,10,10) and B(5,5,10,10). Print true or false.
Test two boxes that do NOT overlap: A(0,0,10,10) and B(50,50,10,10). Print true or false.
exercises.hint: They are far apart, so false.

exercises.q: Two circles: centres 10 apart, radii 6 and 5 (sum 11). Do they touch? Print true or false.
exercises.solution:

console.log(dist < r1+r2);

lessons.title: Score, lives and game state
lessons.content:
Games are made of variables that change

Score, lives, level, "is the game over?" — these are just variables you update on events. The whole "feel" of a game is rules over these variables.

let score = 0;
let lives = 3;
let gameOver = false;

function onCatchFruit(){ score += 1; }
function onMiss(){ lives -= 1; if (lives === 0) gameOver = true; }

lessons.title: Keyboard controls (the logic)
lessons.content:
Turning key presses into movement

A key press just sets a direction. The classic rule in Snake: you may turn, but you can't instantly reverse into yourself.

// direction is {x, y}. 'up' is {x:0, y:-1}
function setDir(key, dir){
  const map = {up:{x:0,y:-1}, down:{x:0,y:1}, left:{x:-1,y:0}, right:{x:1,y:0}};
  const nd = map[key];
  // reject a reverse (opposite of current)
  if (nd && !(nd.x === -dir.x && nd.y === -dir.y)) return nd;
  return dir;
}

exercises.q: Moving right is {x:1,y:0}. Print the x and y for pressing up (0 and -1), on two lines.
exercises.starter:

// print up.x then up.y

exercises.q: You are moving right (dir {x:1,y:0}). Pressing left would reverse. Print 'blocked' if the new dir is the exact opposite, else 'ok'.
exercises.solution:

if(nd.x===-dir.x && nd.y===-dir.y){ console.log('blocked'); } else { console.log('ok'); }

exercises.q: Same setup but pressing up {x:0,y:-1} while moving right — that's a legal turn. Print 'ok' or 'blocked'.
exercises.starter:
let dir = {x:1, y:0};
let nd = {x:0, y:-1};   // up
exercises.hint: up is not the opposite of right, so ok.
exercises.solution:

if(nd.x===-dir.x && nd.y===-dir.y){ console.log('blocked'); } else { console.log('ok'); }

lessons.title: Simple enemy AI: chase the player
lessons.content:
The simplest 'AI': move toward the target

A chasing enemy just compares its position to the player's and steps one unit closer on each axis. That is enough to feel alive.

function step(enemy, player){
  if (player.x > enemy.x) enemy.x += 1;
  else if (player.x < enemy.x) enemy.x -= 1;
  if (player.y > enemy.y) enemy.y += 1;
  else if (player.y < enemy.y) enemy.y -= 1;
}

Better enemies add patrols, line-of-sight and pathfinding — but they all build on this idea.

exercises.q: Enemy at x=0, player at x=5. Step the enemy toward the player 3 times. Print the enemy x.
exercises.starter:

// 3 steps toward player

exercises.q: Enemy at (2,2), player at (2,6). Move the enemy one step toward the player, then print its y.
The enemy catches the player when they share a position. Enemy (4,4), player (4,4). Print 'caught' or 'chasing'.
exercises.starter:

// same spot?
exercises.solution:

if(e.x===p.x && e.y===p.y){ console.log('caught'); } else { console.log('chasing'); }
